source.title: Adversarial robustness guarantees for random deep neural networks
source.authors: Giacomo De Palma; B. Kiani; S. Lloyd

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices and experimental details.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures adversarial distances for random and trained networks, not training classification error, local minima, training stability, or training speed as described by the versions. Its training-related accuracy figures do not measure training error reaching or failing to reach zero.
record.gate_note: No rows qualify for V1–V6. The paper reports training and test accuracy for MNIST and CIFAR10 networks, but the claim versions concern training error behavior under the specified settings; those accuracy results do not establish that behavior. Adversarial-distance experiments do not measure the claim's subject.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own training accuracy for a randomly initialized convolutional residual network trained with Adam on binary CIFAR-10. Its 98.8% training accuracy equals 1.2% training classification error and bears on V1 in this modified task, despite the paper's focus on adversarial robustness.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors establish probabilistic adversarial-distance guarantees for random networks, validate the predicted scaling experimentally, and find trained-network results mostly consistent. Extension to SGD-trained networks remains conjectural and would require assumptions on training data; the Bayesian result holds under a specified matching target-function prior.
record.recipe_differences: The experiments examine adversarial distances of random networks and networks trained on MNIST or CIFAR10, rather than the training-error behaviors specified in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and input type affect the reported adversarial distances: MNIST and CIFAR10 results differ, as do random, training-set, and test-set images.

fits_no_version.finding: Adversarial distances scale with input dimension in random networks; training changes those distances differently on MNIST and CIFAR-10.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial robustness and distance to classification boundaries depend on input dimension, training, and dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: The binary MNIST network achieves average training accuracy of 99.8% after 15 epochs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adam can achieve near-zero training error on binary MNIST with this residual architecture.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 139, 2021)
record.problems: The training experiments report adversarial distances and accuracy, not training classification error. They use binary classification tasks and a simplified residual architecture for the summarized experiments; trained-network distance results are presented in figures. The paper notes that CIFAR10 training and test accuracy differ by 16.3%.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying rows for the claim versions. Adversarial-distance measurements and training/test accuracy results in Sections 4.1, E.3, and Figures 3–4 do not measure the outcomes named by V1–V6.

untested.parts: Standard ten-class CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, width dependence, early-stopping comparisons, and regularization comparisons.
All: teacher-student optimization, spurious local minima, and surplus student neurons.
All: training-error comparisons across depth and identity-shortcut conditions.
All: initialization comparisons measuring training speed or trainable depth.
All: stability thresholds, loss-curvature dynamics, recovery, and divergence.
All: normalization comparisons measuring training speed or learning-rate tolerance, including Fixup.

missing.what: Add the binary CIFAR-10 training result: average training accuracy 98.8%, equivalent to 1.2% training classification error, after 25 epochs with Adam at 0.0001. The record explicitly excludes this result, but its stated justification is incorrect: training accuracy directly determines training classification error.
missing.locator: Appendix E.3, Trained Networks; architecture in Table 2 and initialization in Appendix E.2.

record.verdict_notes: The binary CIFAR-10 result supports only the tested task. No comparison establishes depth, initialization, or normalization effects. The 16.3 percentage-point training–test accuracy gap concerns generalization, not failure to optimize training error.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error, label corruption, random labels, model size, early stopping, and regularized recipes.
Teacher-student local minima and student width relative to teacher width.
Depth, residual shortcuts, plain-network training error, and normalization comparisons.
Initialization effects on learning speed or trainable depth.
Learning-rate stability, loss and curvature dynamics, and divergence.
Batch-normalization effects on training speed or learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.

relationships.condition: Binary CIFAR-10; simplified residual CNN; Adam at learning rate 0.0001 for 25 epochs, without batch normalization or dropout.
relationships.reason: Appendix E.3 reports average training accuracy of 98.8%, equivalent to near-zero training error of 1.2%; this verdict rests on the text because the record contains no rows.
relationships.display_finding: Average training accuracy reached 98.8%, corresponding to 1.2% training error.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
